content: 1. A high-fiber diet can help soften stools and make them easier to pass, thereby reducing the strain on hemorrhoids caused by excessive straining during defecation. 2. Dietary fiber is not digested in the gastrointestinal tract but plays a crucial role in improving digestion and preventing constipation. 3. Excellent sources of dietary fiber include fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. 4. Bulk stool softeners or fiber supplements, such as psyllium (Metamucil) or methylcellulose (Citrucel), may be beneficial in managing hemorrhoidal symptoms. 5. Topical analgesics, such as 5% lidocaine ointment, are used to alleviate pain associated with complicated hemorrhoids. 6. Lidocaine works by blocking sodium channels in sensory nerve endings, thereby inhibiting the propagation of pain signals. 7. Topical anti-inflammatory agents combined with cortisone can be used to reduce inflammation and shrink the size of hemorrhoids. 8. Cortisone-containing agents should not be used for more than one month, as prolonged use may suppress local immunity and lead to the development of skin tags. 9. Sitz baths can be effective in relieving pruritus (itching) associated with hemorrhoids. 10. Hydroxyethylrutoside is a venotonic agent that enhances the tone of rectal veins, improves venous and lymphatic flow, alleviates symptoms, and reduces the incidence of bleeding. 11. Local nitroglycerin can be used as an antispasmodic to relieve spasms associated with hemorrhoidal pain. 12. Hemorrhoids can be classified as internal or external. 13. Internal hemorrhoids are located above the dentate line and result from the dilation of the superior hemorrhoidal plexus. 14. The connective tissue overlying the superior hemorrhoidal plexus is innervated by visceral nerves, making it insensitive to pain. 15. External hemorrhoids are located below the dentate line and arise from the dilation of the inferior hemorrhoidal plexus. 16. The initial step in the pathogenesis of both types of hemorrhoids involves the weakening of the surrounding connective tissue and vein walls. 17. Risk factors such as advanced age, pregnancy, and portal hypertension exacerbate this weakness or increase internal venous pressure, worsening the condition. 18. Increased tone of the internal anal sphincter can cause feces to press against the hemorrhoid, reducing venous return and aggravating symptoms. 19. Arteriovenous anastomoses may contribute to the development of hemorrhoids, as evidenced by the improvement of some hemorrhoids after ligation of connecting arteries. 20. The redundant, bulging mucosa in hemorrhoids is prone to injury, leading to bleeding. The blood is typically bright red, reflecting its high oxygen content due to the proximity of arteriovenous anastomoses. 21. Chronic constipation can irritate hemorrhoids due to the passage of hard stools. 22. Excessive consumption of dairy products, such as cheese, can lead to an overproduction of lactic acid in the stool, causing irritation. Reducing the intake of these foods may provide relief. 23. Vitamin E deficiency is also a common contributing factor to hemorrhoidal irritation. 24. Consuming probiotic-rich foods, such as yogurt with active cultures, or eating fruits can help maintain normal gut function and prevent flare-ups of hemorrhoidal symptoms. 25. The use of unnatural sitting toilets has been implicated in the development of hemorrhoids, as evidenced by their low incidence in populations that use squatting toilets. 26. In 1987, Dr. Berko Sikirov conducted a study in which hemorrhoid sufferers switched to squatting toilets. Eighteen out of twenty patients experienced complete relief from symptoms (pain and bleeding) with no recurrence, even 30 months after the study concluded. 27. However, no follow-up studies have been published to confirm these findings. 28. The American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons has not issued any recommendations regarding the therapeutic value of squatting for hemorrhoid management.
